prompt.context_jp: 舞台の上では朱雀部長____マイクを握り直し、締めの挨拶に入ろうとしている。

feedback.correct_en: The scene opens with the narrator spotting Suzaku on stage — he is new information in the visual frame, so が introduces him as the newly perceived subject.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would mark Suzaku as an already-established topic, but here the camera is sweeping onto him for the first time in this scene; he is not yet the running topic.

contrast_examples.jp: 向こうから部長が来た。
contrast_examples.en: Here comes 部長 (new in view) — が.

contrast_examples.jp: 部長はまだ会議中だ。
contrast_examples.en: As for 部長 (already-known topic), he's still in a meeting — は.

prompt.context_jp: 汗と熱気の匂いがまだ残るホールに、部長の朗々とした声____響き渡る。

feedback.correct_en: The voice emerges into the hall as a fresh sensory event — が marks it as newly arriving information that fills the space.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame the voice as the already-established topic being discussed, but here the sentence paints a scene where the voice suddenly rings out.

contrast_examples.jp: 遠くで鐘が鳴った。
contrast_examples.en: A bell rang in the distance (event arrival) — が.

contrast_examples.jp: その声は低く落ち着いていた。
contrast_examples.en: The voice (known topic) was low and calm — は.

prompt.context_jp: 雉谷の顔つき____、朝から妙に落ち着き払っている。

feedback.correct_en: The narrator picks out 雉谷の顔つき as the topic being characterized ('as for her expression…'); は fits a general description about an already-identified referent.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would signal that his expression is new, exhaustive information — but here we're commenting on a known person's state, not spotting something new.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の表情は暗かった。
contrast_examples.en: His expression (topic) was dark — は.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の表情が急に変わった。
contrast_examples.en: His expression suddenly changed (new event) — が.

prompt.context_jp: 文字____妙に大きく、色分けも過剰なほど親切で、まるで小学校の配布物のようだ。

feedback.correct_en: The sentence is describing properties of the handout (文字 as topic/aspect), and the following 色分けも parallels it — は sets up this aspect-by-aspect description.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would spotlight the characters as newly noticed, but here Hiwada is enumerating features: 'the text is… the color-coding is also…'

contrast_examples.jp: この資料は字が大きい。
contrast_examples.en: This document — the text is large (describing the known doc) — は / が.

contrast_examples.jp: あっ、字が消えてる！
contrast_examples.en: Oh, the text has disappeared! (sudden notice) — が.

prompt.context_jp: 俺____上司に言われて いちばんイヤな言葉は "聞いてないんだけど"だ

feedback.correct_en: Inside the relative clause 「俺が上司に言われて…言葉」, 俺 is the subject of 言われる and must take が — subordinate-clause subjects normally stay as が, not は.
feedback.incorrect_en: は is reserved for the main-clause topic (here it's attached to 言葉は). Putting は on 俺 would try to make him a second topic inside the modifier, which doesn't work.

contrast_examples.jp: 私が作った料理はおいしい。
contrast_examples.en: The food I made is tasty — subordinate subject takes が.

contrast_examples.jp: 私は料理を作った。
contrast_examples.en: I made food — main-clause topic takes は.

prompt.context_jp: 鶸田____書類の隅をそっと揃えながら、目の前の茶番の全体像をどう捉えたものか分からずにいた。

feedback.correct_en: Hiwada is the ongoing POV character of the narration; は sustains him as the topic whose inner state we're following.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would reintroduce him as new information, as if the reader didn't know he was in the room — but we've been with him the whole scene.

contrast_examples.jp: 鶸田は困っていた。
contrast_examples.en: Hiwada (continuing topic) was troubled — は.

contrast_examples.jp: そこへ鶸田が入ってきた。
contrast_examples.en: Then Hiwada walked in (new on scene) — が.

prompt.context_jp: 朱雀の張り上げる声____すでに上の階から聞こえてくる。

feedback.correct_en: The voice is a newly perceived stimulus reaching them on the staircase — が marks this sudden sensory arrival.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat the voice as the already-established topic, but here it's the fresh event the narrator wants us to notice.

contrast_examples.jp: どこかで赤ちゃんが泣いている。
contrast_examples.en: Somewhere a baby is crying (newly perceived) — が.

contrast_examples.jp: その赤ちゃんは隣の子だ。
contrast_examples.en: That baby (known) is the neighbor's — は.

prompt.context_jp: 誰も目を合わせようとせず、天井のエアコンの音だけ____やけに大きく聞こえる。

feedback.correct_en: だけ excludes everything else, and the only remaining sound is spotlighted — this exhaustive 'nothing but X' reading pairs with が.
feedback.incorrect_en: だけは would add a contrastive 'at least only this one' flavor that doesn't fit a quiet descriptive moment of awkward silence.

contrast_examples.jp: 時計の音だけが聞こえた。
contrast_examples.en: Only the clock could be heard — exhaustive が.

contrast_examples.jp: それだけは言わないで。
contrast_examples.en: Just don't say that one thing (contrastive) — だけは.

prompt.context_jp: 部長の話____どこへ着地するのか、誰にも見当がつかなかった。

feedback.correct_en: Inside the embedded question 「どこへ着地するのか」, 部長の話 is the subject of 着地する; subjects of embedded clauses take が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would try to make 部長の話 a main-clause topic, but the whole clause is itself the object of 見当がつかなかった, so a topic marker breaks the structure.

contrast_examples.jp: 誰が来るか分からない。
contrast_examples.en: I don't know who's coming — embedded subject takes が.

contrast_examples.jp: その話は面白かった。
contrast_examples.en: That story was interesting — main-clause topic は.

prompt.context_jp: 話し合いの流れとは無関係に、彼の眉____次第に険しさを増していった。

feedback.correct_en: 彼の眉 is being characterized as the aspect under narration ('as for his brow, it grew tenser'); は fits this descriptive, ongoing-topic reading.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would mark the brow as newly noticed, but the sentence contrasts the meeting flow with his separate internal state — は carries that contrastive-topic nuance.

contrast_examples.jp: 顔は笑っているが、目は怒っていた。
contrast_examples.en: The face was smiling, but the eyes were angry — contrastive は.

contrast_examples.jp: 顔が真っ赤になった。
contrast_examples.en: The face turned bright red (event) — が.

prompt.context_jp: 午後の営業フロアには、いつもの倦怠感____戻っていた。

feedback.correct_en: The sentence presents a scene: 'there was X on the floor.' 倦怠感 is the newly introduced existent in that scene, so が fits.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame 倦怠感 as a known topic being commented on, but the sentence is painting the scene afresh after the lunchtime episode.

contrast_examples.jp: 部屋に変な匂いがした。
contrast_examples.en: There was a strange smell in the room (new) — が.

contrast_examples.jp: その匂いは古い本の匂いだった。
contrast_examples.en: That smell (known) was of old books — は.

prompt.context_jp: 雉谷の声には、いつもの投げやりさ____微塵もなかった。

feedback.correct_en: The は here is contrastive: 'his usual flippancy — that in particular wasn't there,' implying other qualities were present. It pairs naturally with negative existence.
feedback.incorrect_en: が…なかった is grammatical but neutral; the story is pointedly contrasting this moment with his usual manner, which は highlights.

contrast_examples.jp: お金はないが、時間はある。
contrast_examples.en: I have no money, but I do have time — contrastive は.

contrast_examples.jp: そこにはお金がなかった。
contrast_examples.en: There was no money there (neutral) — が.

prompt.context_jp: 出演したアーティストたちの名前____、一人ずつ噛みしめるように呼び上げていく

feedback.correct_en: 呼び上げる is a transitive verb and 名前 is its direct object — the thing he is calling out. を marks it clearly.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would wrongly make the names the subject (as if they were doing the calling), and は would turn them into a topic that clashes with the following ずつ enumeration.

contrast_examples.jp: 名前を呼ぶ。
contrast_examples.en: Call out a name — direct object を.

contrast_examples.jp: 名前が呼ばれる。
contrast_examples.en: The name is called (passive subject) — が.

prompt.context_jp: 鶸田はその光景を、少し離れた席____茫然と見上げていた。

feedback.correct_en: 見上げる is directional — the gaze travels from his seat up to the stage, so から ('from') captures the vantage point.
feedback.incorrect_en: で would mark the seat as the location of an action generally, but here the focus is on where the gaze originates. に would mark a destination, which doesn't fit 見上げる's source.

contrast_examples.jp: 遠くから見ていた。
contrast_examples.en: Watching from far away — から.

contrast_examples.jp: 遠くで事故があった。
contrast_examples.en: There was an accident far away (location of event) — で.

prompt.context_jp: ホールの隅で椅子に沈み込んだ鶸田____、耳の奥にまだ残る歓声を思い出していた。

feedback.correct_en: The chapter opens by presenting Hiwada and then switching to describe his inner state — は establishes him as the chapter's topic whose thoughts we'll follow.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present Hiwada as newly spotted, but the heavy modifier already locates him in the scene and we move on to his thoughts, which is textbook topic-は territory.

contrast_examples.jp: 主人公は昔を思い出していた。
contrast_examples.en: The protagonist was reminiscing (topic frame) — は.

contrast_examples.jp: そこに主人公が現れた。
contrast_examples.en: The protagonist appeared there (new entrance) — が.

prompt.context_jp: 客席のあちこちで拍手____起こり、社員たちが顔を見合わせて頷き合う。

feedback.correct_en: 拍手が起こる is a presentational event — applause spontaneously breaks out. The sentence reports the new occurrence, so が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat applause as the known topic being commented on, but here the sentence is reporting a sudden happening in the hall.

contrast_examples.jp: 歓声が上がった。
contrast_examples.en: Cheers went up (event) — が.

contrast_examples.jp: その拍手はしばらく続いた。
contrast_examples.en: That applause (known) continued for a while — は.

prompt.context_jp: 鵜飼のもごもごとした返事に、会議室____しんと静まり返った。

feedback.correct_en: 会議室 has just been established as the setting; は picks it up as the topic and tells us what happened to it ('as for the room, it fell silent').
feedback.incorrect_en: が would spotlight the room itself as new information, but the room is the already-given stage; what's new is the silence falling over it.

contrast_examples.jp: 教室はしんと静まった。
contrast_examples.en: The classroom (known setting) fell silent — は.

contrast_examples.jp: 急に会議室が暗くなった。
contrast_examples.en: The room suddenly went dark (event-focused) — が.

prompt.context_jp: 鶸田は「証拠」という言葉の物騒さに戸惑いつつ、その徹底ぶりに____を巻いた。

feedback.correct_en: 舌を巻く is a fixed idiom meaning 'to be astonished / lost for words at someone's skill.' It fits Hiwada's reaction to Kijitani's thoroughness.
feedback.incorrect_en: 手を巻く and 目を巻く are not idioms. 手を焼く (be at a loss handling) or 目を見張る (be wide-eyed) exist, but they don't fit the frame ___を巻いた here.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の記憶力に舌を巻いた。
contrast_examples.en: I was astounded by his memory.

contrast_examples.jp: あの子には手を焼いている。
contrast_examples.en: That kid is a handful.

prompt.context_jp: 俺は絶対に____を外されたくない

feedback.correct_en: ハシゴを外される literally 'to have the ladder pulled out from under you' = to be left in the lurch by someone who urged you on. It fits Kijitani's fear of superiors turning on him.
feedback.incorrect_en: イスを外す/カサを外す aren't idioms. The imagery is specifically the ladder being yanked away after you've climbed up.

contrast_examples.jp: 上司にハシゴを外された。
contrast_examples.en: My boss hung me out to dry.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼に裏切られた。
contrast_examples.en: I was betrayed by him (plain version).

prompt.context_jp: この場においていかなる意見でも出てさえくれば御の字だ、と雉谷は____をくくった。

feedback.correct_en: 腹をくくる means 'to brace oneself / resolve.' Kijitani lowers his expectations and steels himself to accept whatever comes up.
feedback.incorrect_en: 首をくくる literally means 'to hang oneself,' which obviously doesn't fit. 気をくくる is not a standard phrase.

contrast_examples.jp: もうダメだと腹をくくった。
contrast_examples.en: I steeled myself, thinking it was over.

contrast_examples.jp: 気を引き締める。
contrast_examples.en: To tighten one's resolve (different idiom).

prompt.context_jp: ゴルフ場での快進撃がいかにこの会社の力学を狂わせるか、彼には____取るように見えている。

feedback.correct_en: 手に取るように = 'as clearly as if holding it in your hand.' It describes vivid, immediate understanding.
feedback.incorrect_en: 目に見える exists but means 'visible'; it doesn't use the 取る frame. 気に取る isn't an idiom.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の気持ちが手に取るように分かる。
contrast_examples.en: I can read his feelings clear as day.

contrast_examples.jp: 目に見えて成績が上がった。
contrast_examples.en: His grades improved visibly.

prompt.context_jp: モメたくない 面倒事に____たくない一心で できるようになった

feedback.correct_en: 面倒事に巻き込まれる = 'to get dragged into trouble.' Kijitani's whole philosophy is avoiding being pulled into messes, so 巻き込まれたくない fits.
feedback.incorrect_en: 引き受けたくない means 'don't want to take on,' and 立ち向かいたくない 'don't want to confront' — both plausible but neither matches the passive 'swept up in' nuance of 面倒事に.

contrast_examples.jp: 事件に巻き込まれた。
contrast_examples.en: I got caught up in the incident.

contrast_examples.jp: 仕事を引き受けた。
contrast_examples.en: I took on the job (active choice).

prompt.context_jp: 大事なのは 情報の入れ方の____だ

feedback.correct_en: Kijitani's whole scheme was about the sequence of planting information (Kamogawa first, then HR, then Shigiishi) — 順番 captures this ordering strategy.
feedback.incorrect_en: 種類 (kind) and 場所 (place) are plausible nouns, but the point of the trick was timing/order, not what kind or where.

contrast_examples.jp: 話す順番を決める。
contrast_examples.en: Decide the order of speaking.

contrast_examples.jp: 情報の種類を分ける。
contrast_examples.en: Sort information by type.

prompt.context_jp: 「ああ 部長の____」(資料のことを比喩で言う)
prompt.prompt_en: Which word is Kijitani using as a metaphor for the chief's dumbed-down handout?

feedback.correct_en: 離乳食 (baby food) is Kijitani's cutting metaphor: the materials are chewed up and pre-digested because the chief 'can't handle solid food.' That mockery is the whole joke of the scene.
feedback.incorrect_en: お弁当 or ごちそう wouldn't carry the insult. The humor rides on the infantilizing image of 離乳食.

contrast_examples.jp: 離乳食みたいな資料。
contrast_examples.en: A handout like baby food (dumbed-down).

contrast_examples.jp: 豪華なごちそう。
contrast_examples.en: A lavish feast (opposite nuance).

prompt.context_jp: 面倒を避けるために積み上げてきた努力が、いかに____かを彼は初めて意識した。

feedback.correct_en: 脆い (fragile, easily crumbling) matches the realization that his elaborate avoidance tactics collapse the moment real pressure comes.
feedback.incorrect_en: 固い (solid) is the opposite of what he's realizing. 重い (heavy) doesn't fit — the issue is that it falls apart, not that it's burdensome.

contrast_examples.jp: 信頼は脆いものだ。
contrast_examples.en: Trust is a fragile thing.

contrast_examples.jp: 守りが固い。
contrast_examples.en: The defense is solid (opposite).

prompt.context_jp: 「同じ日のうちに取引先ごとに別人のように振る舞う雉谷」の描写として、
prompt.prompt_en: Which sounds more natural as narration?

choices.text: 雉谷の口調は先ほどとはまるで別人のように砕けた。
雉谷の口調はまるで別人のように先ほどと砕けた。

feedback.correct_en: A keeps the comparison 先ほどと ('compared to a moment ago') together with まるで別人のように, producing a clean 'compared-to-X, like-Y' flow before the verb.
feedback.incorrect_en: B splits 先ほどと away from its comparative partner まるで別人のように, leaving 先ほどと夾く dangling awkwardly before 砕けた.

contrast_examples.jp: 昨日とはまるで別人のように優しかった。
contrast_examples.en: He was gentle, like a different person from yesterday — natural order.

contrast_examples.jp: まるで別人のように昨日と優しかった。
contrast_examples.en: Awkward: comparison phrase and comparee are split.

prompt.context_jp: 初対面の大手クライアントに若手として挨拶する場面で、
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds more natural for a junior greeting a big client?

choices.text: 精いっぱい やらせていただきますので どうぞ よろしくお願いいたします
精いっぱい やってやりますので どうぞ よろしくお願いいたします

feedback.correct_en: やらせていただく is humble-form, the standard self-lowering phrase a junior uses before a client. It matches どうぞよろしくお願いいたします.
feedback.incorrect_en: やってやります sounds boastful/confrontational ('I'll do it for you'), clashing badly with the humble closing お願いいたします.

contrast_examples.jp: 担当させていただきます。
contrast_examples.en: I'll (humbly) handle it — client-facing humble.

contrast_examples.jp: やってやるよ。
contrast_examples.en: I'll do it (brash, friends only).

prompt.context_jp: 鳩山が鶸田の誤解を正しつつ、雉谷の行動を説明する場面で、

choices.text: 雉谷くんは ただただ 面倒なことになる前に 早めに手を打ってるだけなの
雉谷くんが ただただ 面倒なことになる前に 早めに手を打ってるだけなの

feedback.correct_en: Hatoyama is explaining what Kijitani (the already-known person Hiwada just asked about) is really up to — は fits this topic-explanation structure.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present Kijitani as newly identified ('it's Kijitani who…'), which conflicts with the explanatory 〜だけなの ending that comments on known behavior.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は困ってるだけだよ。
contrast_examples.en: He's just in trouble, that's all (explanation about him) — は.

contrast_examples.jp: 困ってるのは彼だよ。
contrast_examples.en: It's him who's in trouble (identification) — exhaustive が.

prompt.context_jp: 雉谷が落ち込んでいる後輩の鶸田に、カジュアルに声をかける場面で、
prompt.prompt_en: Which sounds more natural from senpai to kōhai here?

choices.text: 隠さなくていいって お前 分かりやすすぎ とりあえず言ってみ
隠さなくてもよろしいです あなたは分かりやすすぎます とりあえず仰ってください

feedback.correct_en: Kijitani's register with his kōhai is casual-cool: dropped particles, 〜って, お前, imperative 言ってみ. A matches the easy senpai tone.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is overly formal (〜ます/仰る/あなた), which would feel cold or sarcastic between workplace familiars and clash with the comforting intent.

contrast_examples.jp: とりあえず言ってみ。
contrast_examples.en: Just try saying it (casual senpai).

contrast_examples.jp: ひとまずお話しください。
contrast_examples.en: Please share your thoughts (formal/customer-facing).

prompt.context_jp: 雉谷が自分の職業観を語る場面で、

choices.text: 頑張っても報われない
頑張っても応えられない

feedback.correct_en: 報われる is the standard verb for 'effort being rewarded.' 頑張っても報われない is a near-cliché for 'hard work going unrewarded.'
feedback.incorrect_en: 応える means 'respond to (expectations)' — it needs a different frame like 期待に応える. It doesn't collocate with 頑張っても〜ない in this sense.

contrast_examples.jp: 努力が報われた。
contrast_examples.en: My effort paid off.

contrast_examples.jp: 期待に応える。
contrast_examples.en: Live up to expectations (different frame).
